Ratification helped restore Montagnard authority, while wartime emergency postponed implementation; popular approval of the constitution does not prove endorsement of every coercive institution.
Nantes defeats the Vendéan assault.
Girondin sympathy does not compel alignment against the Republic.
Montagnards curb radical allies after the purge.
Frimaire attacks local reinterpretation and representative autonomy.
Local armies are abolished before the Paris army.

relationships.rationale: September pressure drives legislation and revolutionary government.
Robespierre defends worship as a basis of civil order.
Collot and Billaud abolish the justice committee.
Mobilization helped the recovery that reduced the immediate military justification for emergency coercion; Terror nevertheless continued and intensified.
Real financial fraud breaks the moderation alliance.
Moral suspicion contributes to the purge, with motives uncertain.
Potential danger becomes an increasingly important basis for punishment.
Centralization crowds Paris prisons and accelerates procedural reform.
Ceremonial prominence intensifies dictatorship accusations without proving intent.
Recent wage cuts are one of several reasons for popular nonmobilization.
Controls’ abolition aggravated hardship alongside harvest, weather, transport and currency pressures; it was not the sole cause.
Religious conciliation helps negotiate western settlements.
Disarmament and detention expose former terrorists to vengeance.
The defeated rebellion makes the 1793 constitution unacceptable to the Convention.
Official connivance and custody facilitate some private massacres.
The suspended constitution supplies a rallying demand.
Prairial combines constitutional and material demands.
Rival claimants, advisers and incompatible strategies undermined common action; the source presents factionalism as one cause of armed failure alongside localism and foreign priorities.

Constitutional monarchists accepted substantial revolutionary change, whereas Louis XVIII continued to defend a restoration programme; this contrast concerns the constitutional-alternative facet of the programme subject.
Artois authorized La Rouërie’s Breton organization, whose plans nevertheless depended on local networks and were overtaken by events.
Artois’s appointment gave Puisaye a claim to leadership; it did not turn the scattered Breton bands into a unified force.
Louis XVIII rejected concessions required by constitutional monarchists; his restoration policy helped sustain divisions rather than settle them.
British arms and shipping made the Quiberon attempt possible, but divided command and poor coordination helped defeat it.
British support brought Artois to the Île d’Yeu; the expedition never achieved the intended link with mainland insurgents.

Toulon began within the anti-Jacobin provincial revolt, then accepted a conditional royalist and British alignment. Its limited constitutional royalism was an exception to predominantly republican federalist aims.
Puisaye claimed a scale and unity of Breton command that the locally organized guerrillas did not possess.
Puisaye’s representations helped persuade Britain to support a landing, without eliminating British strategic self-interest or the division among royalists.
Mallet du Pan sought accommodation with revolutionary changes; d’Antraigues pursued uncompromising restoration and an intelligence network. Their shared opposition did not imply a common programme.
Captured intelligence exposed Pichegru’s royalist contacts. The evidential claim concerns those contacts, not every activity of Condé’s surviving corps.
Hoche contained and defeated the Quiberon landing, making its failed coordination and the aftermath decisive for western royalist hopes.
Hoche’s 1795–1796 pressure, discipline and accommodation subdued surviving Vendéan insurgency. This is not the destruction of the main Catholic and Royal Army in 1793.
Hoche’s military pressure and selective conciliation weakened Breton resistance, while dispersed bands and local circumstances prevented an instantaneous final settlement.
Military pressure helped induce the provisional western agreements; religious concessions, fatigue and tactical calculations also mattered.
Artois’s island expedition failed to make effective contact with Charette, disappointing a mainland leader who had expected royal and British assistance.
Armed defeat did not extinguish a constitutional route to monarchy. The source separates that surviving political possibility from restoration by invasion or rural war.
Charette’s acceptance of peace was tactical and conditional; it did not establish permanent reconciliation with the Republic.
After Quiberon, Cadoudal became the strongest remaining Breton chief and Puisaye’s authority declined. The source does not make Cadoudal commander of a single unified chouan army.
The government’s victory enabled institutional demobilization of Parisian sectional power, not merely the existence of an uprising.
relationships.target_facet: Abolition of the sections and National Guard

relationships.rationale: The army’s role in defeating the rising helped establish the new regime’s reliance on soldiers.
Hardship, deflation and resentment encouraged renewed Jacobin mobilization, without making all popular discontent Jacobin or communist.
Babeuf’s programme went beyond civil equality toward material equality, opposing the Year III settlement’s identification of property with political competence.
The failure of the Equals was followed by the Grenelle attempt; the latter’s defeat further discredited an insurrectionary strategy rather than proving identical organization.
The elections removed the Directors’ dependable legislative majority and brought a divided executive into conflict with the Councils.
The Fructidor coup enabled renewed repression of returned émigrés, nobles and refractory clergy, with different laws and uneven implementation.
Fructidor removed an opportunity for Austria to exploit divisions in Paris; the strengthened French government and Bonaparte could secure Campo Formio.
After Fructidor, the French demands at Lille hardened beyond what Britain would accept and the talks ended. This outcome differs from the peace concluded with Austria.
The invasion of Egypt and destruction of the French fleet altered Ottoman and Russian calculations and helped produce a new coalition; they were not the only continental grievances.
The prospect of renewed continental war and depleted armies prompted the September 1798 recruitment law; formal war with Austria followed in March 1799.
relationships.source_facet: Prospect of renewed coalition war in 1798

relationships.rationale: The continuity law angered opponents of the Convention and helped provoke Vendémiaire; the uprising was not uniformly royalist.
Abolition of sectional assemblies and their National Guard removed the machinery of the traditional mass journée, encouraging the Equals to plan seizure through a smaller conspiracy.

Debt cancellation reduced the state’s obligations while tax-administration reforms sought more dependable receipts. They are complementary fiscal measures, not identical policies or a demonstrated single-step institutional cause.
relationships.source_facet: Cancellation of two thirds of the funded debt
relationships.target_facet: Rebuilding of taxation and revenue administration

relationships.rationale: The Directory initially permitted Jacobin activity to counter royalism, then suppressed threats from that quarter; its later collapse was not the cause of the earlier revival.
relationships.source_facet: Early Jacobin revival and organization under the Directory
relationships.target_facet: Directorial tolerance as part of balancing against royalism

relationships.rationale: Constitutional circles revived Jacobin organization and helped create an electoral challenge which the Directors suppressed through Floréal.
Clichy deputies, philanthropic institutes, journalism and differing monarchist currents helped organize the Year V challenge without constituting a unified restoration party.
The triumvirs chose a military coup to settle executive-legislative conflict. Doyle treats accommodation as a possible alternative, not the coup as constitutionally inevitable.
The Directorial Terror included oath requirements, detention and deportation of nonjuror priests, whose enforcement and human consequences varied by place.
Post-Floréal confidence and coercive Great Nation expansion multiplied foreign grievances and contributed to renewed coalition war.
French intervention and the extension of client republics, including Switzerland, Rome and Naples, aggravated foreign anxieties and helped form the coalition.
Bonaparte supplied political pressure from his army and Augereau’s military assistance to the triumvirs; this was a concrete contribution to Fructidor.
Political disengagement helps explain limited resistance to Floréal. Quiet does not establish approval of the annulled electoral result.
Indemnities and requisitions supplied money which the government could not reliably raise at home, increasing its dependence on commanders controlling conquered resources.
Pichegru’s treason furnished evidence used against the royalists, but did not prove that an immediate restoration by a unified majority was likely or that Fructidor was necessary.
Commissioners, administrative changes and official pressure attempted to shape the 1797 elections, but did not prevent the hostile result.
Official interference and manipulation of electoral assemblies preceded the Year VI annulments; the government rejected returns it had failed to control.
The Batavian case shows constitutional conflict and French intervention within the sister-republic system, with local political initiative as well as external pressure.
France imposed a centralized Helvetic constitution amid Swiss reform initiatives and opposition grounded in local democratic and religious liberties.
The Roman constitution explicitly subordinated the republic to French military authority, making constrained sovereignty unusually visible.
Fiscal extraction and occupation burdens contributed to hostility alongside religious, local and social conflicts; the Year VII risings were not a uniform national movement.
News of French reverses and the collapse of client states encouraged Bonaparte to leave Egypt; his departure also served personal political calculation.
The United Irishmen organized rebellion and sought French aid, but divided elite, peasant and French aims, disrupted leadership and limited intervention help explain failure.
Prairial opened a temporary opportunity for Jacobin organization and emergency demands; subsequent executive containment reversed that opening.
Jacobin pressure helped produce the forced loan and Law of Hostages through the Councils; later Consular repeal must remain a separate phase.
Under pressure from the Jacobin revival, the Councils activated recruitment under the existing Jourdan law; the movement was not itself the legislative authority.
Bonaparte’s combination of military strength, negotiation and incentives neutralized much renewed chouan resistance, without implying uniform or unconditional royalist acceptance.
Sieyes blocked the Jacobins’ renewed political challenge; this is political containment, not set inclusion or elimination of every earlier Jacobin phase.
Bonaparte’s return supplied Sieyes with the military partner needed for constitutional change, although their subsequent designs for executive power diverged.
Brumaire overthrew the Directory; its success belongs to the collapse sequence which Doyle explains through political conduct and lost legitimacy as well as war.
The preparation of a civil code offered more predictable rules protecting property and civil life, contributing to reconciliation with proprietors.
Opposition to early civil-code proposals formed part of the legislative resistance which Bonaparte answered by purging the Tribunate and Legislative Body.
Religious pragmatism and recognition of Catholic persistence opened negotiations with Pius VII; a simple expectation of religious disappearance had proved untenable.
The Organic Articles imposed Gallican controls while the remaking of the episcopate strengthened papal authority. The negotiated Concordat and unilateral additions were distinct.

The settlement restored public Catholic worship and helped stabilize the regime, culminating symbolically in Easter 1802. It did not erase the lasting Catholic-republican polarization discussed on page 398.
The legislative purge removed opponents before the religious settlement was enacted and publicly celebrated, linking political coercion with the appearance of reconciliation.
Conscription fed resentment and evasion which royalists exploited around Toulouse; the uprising also drew on local political and social conditions.
Renewed recruitment helped reactivate western resistance in autumn 1799; it was one element in dispersed chouan mobilization.
Draft evasion contributed to brigandage and rural disorder confronting the Consulate. It was not a sufficient explanation of all rural crime.
The revolutionary assault on the French Church helped clear the way for a settlement giving Rome a stronger institutional role, despite the clergy’s great material and cultural losses.
relationships.source_facet: Destruction of the old Gallican institutional balance

relationships.rationale: Wartime emancipation encouraged Toussaint’s republican alignment and strengthened black military forces; armed resistance and black power had begun before metropolitan abolition.

Haiti emerged directly from colonial revolution and resistance to restored slavery; Latin America drew revolutionary language and examples through a different process intensified by the later collapse of Spanish authority.

The collapse of paper revenue and deflation intensified tax failure and fiscal desperation before the bankruptcy. This is a setting for repudiation, not a claim that deflation alone dictated the policy.
Expanded resources support recovery without sufficing alone.
The civic cult gives religious expression to republican virtue. This differs from the festival increasing suspicions of personal dictatorship.
Robespierre initially protected Danton and Desmoulins against excessive repression; this temporary alliance must not be conflated with his subsequent framing of their purge.
Evidence of Fabre’s fraud damaged the alignment between Robespierre and the Indulgents; real corruption must remain distinct from fabricated foreign conspiracy.
The defeat at Marseilles helped propel Toulon toward seeking British protection. This is an event sequence, not a claim that both cities shared a royalist programme.
Revolutionary armies requisitioned provisions and coerced suspected hoarders. The edge concerns enforcement of subsistence policy, not all wage or currency policy.
Once immediate military crisis eased, Danton and Desmoulins urged moderation. This scoped late-1793 shift does not make every aspect of Terror a cause of indulgence.
Release and memories of Year II repression supplied revenge motives; the geographically varied White Terror was not wholly royalist or caused by release alone.

The forced loan withdrew purchasing power and contributed to temporary assignat recovery within the controlled economy. Do not attribute this realized effect to the unimplemented Ventôse confiscation scheme.
Virtue and preventive suspicion help explain the treatment of potential enemies in the Great Terror; this is not sole personal authorship or socially indiscriminate killing.
Babeuf used the unimplemented democratic constitution against Thermidorian retreat before the Directory conspiracy.
Toulon workers mobilized against persecution but were defeated and executed. This responsive action differs from the same unit’s account of authorities enabling White Terror.
Inflation, provision shortages and demands for controls sharpened sectional pressure on representation. Keep the 1793 political mobilization distinct from 1794 wage alienation.
Summer danger helped prompt the August levée en masse. Rebind the old compound levy endpoint to the August measure, excluding February conscription and later retrospective mass-war synthesis.
Desmoulins and the Indulgents attacked Hébertist excess, amid reciprocal factional hostility; disagreement is not proof of the alleged foreign plots.
Robespierre supported governmental control and resisted religious coercion; rebind the old religious fragment to his political role rather than treating religion itself as an administrative actor.

The general’s betrayal sharpened the emergency that produced the Committee of Public Safety; this specifically preserves the institution’s creation rather than only the broader emergency-government consequence.
Government consolidation addressed dispersed and self-sustaining coercion; centralization did not simply abolish Terror, and could intensify its use.
Final 1795 repression extinguished organized sansculotte force. Scope this edge to that final result, not the earlier erosion that helped defeat Hébert or Germinal.
Thermidorian measures curtailed committee powers, judicial terror and local emergency organs; the coup-to-dismantling edge alone does not name the institutional object.
February conscription sparked western rural resistance with distinct Breton guerrilla development; it must not be rebound to August national mobilization.
Isolation, absences and fear of further denunciation helped produce the coalition against Robespierre; perceptions of dictatorship are not evidence of unlimited effective power.
The label federalist arose within disputes over legitimate national sovereignty; many rebels professed the same indivisible republic and did not seek federal government.
Exceptional interference with Danton’s defense foreshadowed the later law’s restriction of defendants’ protections; the earlier trial did not occur under that later law.

new_relationships.rationale: Pressure to restrain religious coercion was one motive for central government control; this specific religious connection is not exhausted by the broader Terror-centralization edge.
Restriction of popular institutions and radical leadership weakened independent sansculotte capacity before the final repression of Prairial 1795. Preserve the earlier erosion as a distinct process.

Defeat of Vendémiaire allowed the continuity arrangements to be carried through and former Convention members to retain legislative predominance. This consequence is distinct from the law helping provoke the rising.
Quelling domestic revolts absorbed forces in autumn 1793 and delayed the full effect of mass mobilization on the foreign fronts. This constraint differs from the emergency prompting recruitment.
Debt repudiation inflicted severe creditor losses; the accompanying fiscal reconstruction also alienated the property-owning constituency the Directory wished to secure.

new_relationships.target_facet: Loss of support among property holders
